ei.title: Getbol: A Treasure House with Great Potential
ei.subject: 영어2

fullPassage: Getbol, a Symbol of Biodiversity Have you ever visited the Korean tidal flats known as getbol? Getbol is a muddy and flat environment that is exposed at low tide and is covered by water at high tide. Soil on land has flowed into the sea and accumulated for more than 8,500 years, creating one of the thickest tidal layers in the world. Since the soil includes organic matter from land animals and plants, getbol is rich in nutrients and provides habitats for thousands of species. In fact, getbol is home to approximately 2,150 species of plants and animals, including 22 globally threatened or near-threatened species. Thanks to its rich biodiversity, getbol is visited by about 118 species of migratory birds every year. For millions of migratory birds that travel between Australia and the Russian Far East or Alaska, Korea’s tidal flats are a vital stopover location. Without getbol, they would not have a place to rest and feed themselves during their long journeys, and they would become extinct. Since getbol is not only a unique ecosystem crowded with diverse species but also a resting place for endangered birds, it was added to the UNESCO World Natural Heritage List in 2021. The list includes the four tidal flats on the western and southern coasts of Korea: Seocheon Getbol, Gochang Getbol, Shinan Getbol, and Boseong-Suncheon Getbol. Climate Change and Carbon When people think of a changing climate, images of melting glaciers and polar bears losing their habitat often come to mind. But this is only one aspect of the problem. Climate change is causing extreme weather conditions, which have become more frequent and intense worldwide. Heatwaves, droughts, floods, and wildfires are affecting countries around the world. In the autumn of 2019, for example, Australia was hit by one of the worst wildfires on record. Over six months, the wildfires burned about 10 million hectares of land, and killed hundreds of millions of animals. Approximately 30 percent of the koalas in the region are said to have been killed due to the fires. This is why the international community has been seeking solutions to the climate crisis. In 2015, 195 countries signed the Paris Agreement to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. The countries agreed upon the fact that the increase in atmospheric carbon is a major reason for climate change. One key strategy to combat it is to achieve “carbon neutrality,” which involves maintaining a balance between the amount of carbon emitted and carbon absorbed. The Earth’s Atmosphere Is Like a Bathtub Let’s imagine that the Earth’s atmosphere is a large bathtub, and the greenhouse gases emitted into the atmosphere are like water flowing from a tap into the bathtub. At the bottom of the bathtub, there’s a drain that lets the water out. If we keep the tap running, the water level in the bathtub will rise, just as greenhouse gas emissions have led to an increase in atmospheric carbon. This rise in carbon levels has already resulted in negative environmental consequences, such as climate change. To make matters worse, if the water is not effectively drained, the bathtub will overflow. In other words, if we don't reduce carbon emissions sufficiently, atmospheric carbon will continue to accumulate. Blue Carbon and Getbol One of the most promising ways to reduce carbon in the atmosphere is to use the “good” carbon on Earth. The Earth’s carbon can be divided into three types: black carbon, green carbon, and blue carbon. Black carbon is released while burning fossil fuels, such as coal, oil, and gas. It causes the greenhouse effect, leading to global warming and climate change. Green carbon, on the other hand, is carbon absorbed by and stored in land ecosystems, such as rainforests like the Amazon in South America. It plays a vital role in maintaining the ecosystem because it absorbs carbon dioxide through photosynthesis. Finally, blue carbon is the carbon stored in the ocean, including coastal and marine ecosystems such as mangrove wetlands, seagrass beds, and tidal marshes. The carbon absorption rate of marine ecosystems is about 50 times faster than that of land ecosystems. Blue carbon can store up to 10 times more carbon per unit area than forests on land, making it highly cost-effective. A notable example of blue carbon can be found in tidal flats located around the ocean. Research conducted in 2021 has revealed that getbol in Korea stores approximately 13 million tons of carbon and absorbs over 260,000 tons of carbon dioxide each year. This means that getbol alone can offset the carbon dioxide emissions produced by 110,000 cars in a year. Considering that getbol contains numerous organisms and marine animals that store carbon, the treasure house of blue carbon has become a promising and sustainable solution to the current environmental problem. Scientists worldwide are continuing to explore the capabilities of tidal flats with the goal of having them officially recognized as blue carbon. Efforts to Protect Getbol Getbol in Korea was once considered useless muddy land, so much of it has been reclaimed for farming and urbanization. This has led to a decline in the area of tidal flats, causing a loss of biodiversity. To prevent further damage to the marine ecosystem, both the government and environmental organizations have been making efforts to protect the tidal flats by regulating unnecessary development. Without further efforts to restore getbol, we would fail to preserve this valuable ecosystem for future generations. Read More Green Your Inbox Email is one of the most widely used forms of communication today. Did you know that the seemingly innocent act of looking through emails or checking your inbox has an environmental impact? In reality, email travels through an energy-consuming network, contributing to climate change on our planet. Storing countless email messages in data centers creates carbon emissions. These data centers rely on huge servers to store and access data at all times. Because the centers use electricity to run the servers and to cool down the large amounts of heat that they generate, they consume a significant amount of fossil fuels. Mike Berners-Lee, the British researcher and author of How Bad Are Bananas?: The Carbon Footprint of Everything, looked at our average email traffic. For example, a short phone-to-phone email has a carbon footprint of 0.2g of CO₂ emissions. But, a long email, which takes about ten minutes to write and three minutes to read on a computer, has a footprint of 17g of CO₂ emissions. So, something as simple as deleting unnecessary email messages can help to save the Earth.

✅ ① making: 'Blue carbon can store ~, ___ it highly cost-effective'에서 블루카본이 그것을 비용 효율적으로 '만드는' 능동 관계이므로 분사구문의 현재분사 making이 적절

❌ ④ producing → produced: 'the carbon dioxide emissions ___ by 110,000 cars'에서 배출물은 자동차에 '의해 배출되는' 수동 관계다. 따라서 능동의 현재분사 producing이 아니라 과거분사 produced가 맞다 ← 정답

questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?

det.korean: ② emitted → absorbed: 그린카본은 육상 생태계에 '흡수되어' 저장되는 탄소이므로 absorbed
det.analysis:
✅ ① released: 'Black carbon is released while burning fossil fuels'에서 블랙카본은 화석 연료를 태울 때 '방출되는' 탄소이므로 released가 적절

❌ ② emitted → absorbed: 'Green carbon ~ is carbon ___ by and stored in land ecosystems'에서 그린카본은 육상 생태계에 '흡수되어' 저장되는 탄소다. 방출을 뜻하는 emitted는 정반대이므로 absorbed가 맞다 ← 정답

✅ ③ vital: 'plays a vital role in maintaining the ecosystem'에서 '중요한' 역할이라는 문맥에 적절

✅ ④ absorbs: 'it absorbs carbon dioxide through photosynthesis'에서 광합성으로 이산화탄소를 '흡수한다'는 문맥에 적절
det.tip: absorbed(흡수된) ↔ emitted(방출된). 그린카본은 흡수·저장되는 탄소

questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?

det.korean: ③ abundant → extinct: 갯벌이 없으면 철새들이 쉴 곳을 잃어 '멸종하게' 되므로 extinct
det.analysis:
✅ ① provides: 'getbol ~ provides habitats for thousands of species'에서 서식지를 '제공한다'는 문맥에 적절

✅ ② biodiversity: 'Thanks to its rich biodiversity'에서 풍부한 '생물 다양성' 덕분이라는 문맥에 적절

❌ ③ abundant → extinct: 'Without getbol, they would ~ become ___'에서 갯벌이 없으면 철새들이 쉬고 먹을 곳을 잃으므로 '멸종하게(extinct)' 된다. '풍부해진다(abundant)'는 정반대이므로 extinct가 맞다 ← 정답

✅ ④ endangered: 'a resting place for endangered birds'에서 '멸종 위기의' 새들의 쉼터라는 문맥에 적절
det.tip: extinct(멸종한) ↔ abundant(풍부한). 갯벌 없으면 철새는 멸종

questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 빈칸에 maintaining a balance(균형을 유지하는 것)가 적절
det.analysis:
✅ ① maintaining a balance(균형을 유지하는 것): '탄소 중립'은 배출되는 탄소량과 흡수되는 탄소량 '사이의 균형을 유지하는 것'을 뜻하므로 적절 ← 정답

❌ ② creating a shortage(부족을 만드는 것): 균형이 아니라 부족을 말하므로 문맥에 맞지 않음

❌ ③ ignoring the difference(차이를 무시하는 것): 균형을 유지한다는 개념과 반대

❌ ④ increasing the emissions(배출을 늘리는 것): 탄소를 줄이려는 흐름과 정반대
det.tip: carbon neutrality(탄소 중립) = 배출량과 흡수량 사이의 균형 유지

questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 빈칸에 continue to accumulate(계속 쌓이다)가 적절
det.analysis:
❌ ① gradually disappear(서서히 사라지다): 욕조가 넘치는 비유와 정반대로, 탄소가 줄어든다는 뜻이라 맞지 않음

❌ ② become much cleaner(훨씬 깨끗해지다): 탄소가 계속 늘어난다는 흐름과 반대

✅ ③ continue to accumulate(계속 쌓이다): 배수구로 물이 충분히 빠지지 않으면 욕조가 넘치듯이, 탄소 배출을 충분히 줄이지 않으면 대기 중 탄소가 '계속 쌓인다'가 자연스러움 ← 정답

❌ ④ stop increasing(증가를 멈추다): 배출을 줄이지 않는 상황이므로 증가가 멈춘다는 것은 문맥에 어긋남
det.tip: the bathtub will overflow(욕조가 넘친다) → atmospheric carbon will continue to accumulate(탄소가 계속 쌓인다)
